parts:
Yes. 👍 I’m assuming by **“this”** you mean the **FinGPT paper you uploaded: _FinGPT: Open-Source Financial Large Language Models_**.

And I think this paper is **very important for your stock AI project**, because it gives us the blueprint for the **AI/LLM part** of the application—not the whole stock-prediction system.

Let's learn it properly, from zero, like a course.

---

# 📚 FinGPT — Lesson 1

## 1. First, what problem is this paper trying to solve?

Imagine we have a normal LLM:

```text
Llama / GPT / Mistral
        ↓
     User asks
        ↓
"Why did Tesla fall today?"
```

A general LLM knows language, but finance is special.

The paper identifies three major problems:

### Problem 1 — Finance changes VERY quickly

For example:

```text
10:00 AM
Company announces bad earnings

        ↓

10:01 AM
Stock starts falling

        ↓

10:05 AM
New analyst report

        ↓

10:10 AM
Stock falls further
```

Financial information has **high temporal sensitivity**. The paper emphasizes that market-moving information can have a very short useful window. fileciteturn2file0L53-L64

---

### Problem 2 — Finance is constantly changing

Every day we get:

```text
News
Tweets
Reddit posts
Company announcements
Earnings
Economic data
Stock prices
Analyst opinions
```

So you can't just train an LLM once and say:

> Done. The model knows finance.

The paper explicitly focuses on this dynamic nature of financial information. fileciteturn2file0L55-L64

---

### Problem 3 — Tons of noise

Suppose you collect 1 million tweets:

```text
"TSLA 🚀🚀🚀"

"Tesla going moon"

"I hate Tesla"

"Buy buy buy"

"Tesla earnings..."

"Bro this stock is trash 😂"
```

Not all of this is useful.

This is the **low signal-to-noise ratio** problem.

The useful information is buried inside a huge amount of irrelevant information. fileciteturn2file0L61-L64

---

# 2. So what is FinGPT?

The simplest definition:

> **FinGPT = an open-source framework for adapting LLMs to financial tasks.**

The important word is **framework**.

It isn't simply:

```text
"Here is one magical stock prediction model."
```

Instead:

```text
              FinGPT
                 │
     ┌───────────┼────────────┐
     │           │            │
 Data         LLM          Applications
     │           │            │
 News       Fine-tuning    Sentiment
 Prices     LoRA           Robo-advisor
 Filings    RAG             Trading
 Social     etc.            Analysis
```

The paper explicitly describes FinGPT as an end-to-end framework built around data, engineering, LLMs, tasks, and applications. fileciteturn2file0L83-L98

---

# 3. The BIG idea of the paper

This is the most important thing I want you to understand.

Most beginners think:

> "I need a better AI model."

FinGPT says:

> **The data pipeline is extremely important.**

Think:

```text
              AI MODEL
                  ↑
                  │
              DATA
                  ↑
                  │
         DATA PIPELINE
                  ↑
                  │
        DATA SOURCES
```

If your data is garbage:

```text
Garbage data
     ↓
Amazing LLM
     ↓
Garbage output
```

😂

So FinGPT follows a **data-centric approach**, emphasizing acquisition, cleaning and preprocessing of financial data. fileciteturn2file0L69-L78

---

# 4. The FinGPT architecture

This is the part you should memorize.

The paper has these major layers:

```text
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│       APPLICATIONS          │
│                             │
│ Robo-advisor                │
│ Trading                     │
│ Sentiment Analysis          │
│ Portfolio                   │
└──────────────▲──────────────┘
               │
┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
│            LLM              │
│                             │
│ Llama                       │
│ Mistral                     │
│ etc.                        │
└──────────────▲──────────────┘
               │
┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
│     DATA ENGINEERING        │
│                             │
│ Cleaning                    │
│ Tokenization                │
│ Embeddings                  │
│ Feature extraction          │
│ RAG                         │
└──────────────▲──────────────┘
               │
┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
│       DATA SOURCES          │
│                             │
│ News                        │
│ Social media                │
│ Filings                     │
│ Market data                 │
│ Trends                      │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

That's basically the heart of the paper.

---

# 5. DATA SOURCE layer

This is where your application starts.

The paper discusses several sources.

### 📰 Financial news

Examples:

```text
Reuters
CNBC
Yahoo Finance
```

These contain:

```text
Company news
Earnings
Economic events
Market updates
```

fileciteturn3file0L57-L75

---

### 🐦 Social media

Examples:

```text
Twitter/X
Reddit
Weibo
```

These can provide:

```text
Public sentiment
Investor discussions
Trending topics
Immediate reactions
```

fileciteturn3file0L65-L67

---

### 📄 Company filings

For example:

```text
Annual reports
Quarterly reports
Financial statements
Insider transactions
Company announcements
```

These are particularly valuable because they're more structured and authoritative than random social-media posts. The paper highlights regulatory filings and exchange data as important sources. fileciteturn3file0L68-L72

---

### 🔥 Trends

Things like:

```text
Google Trends
Financial forums
Analyst discussions
```

can provide additional context. fileciteturn3file0L73-L75

---

# 6. Now apply this to YOUR application

Suppose your user searches:

```text
TCS
```

Your system should collect:

```text
                 TCS
                  │
      ┌───────────┼────────────┐
      ↓           ↓            ↓
   Prices       News         Social
      │           │            │
      ↓           ↓            ↓
    OHLCV       Articles     Posts
```

Then:

```text
                 ↓

          DATA ENGINEERING

                 ↓

      Clean + Normalize + Extract

                 ↓

        AI / ML Processing

                 ↓

           User Dashboard
```

Now you're thinking like the paper.

---

# 7. Data Engineering

This is one of the most important parts.

You don't directly send raw internet data to your LLM.

Instead:

```text
RAW DATA
   ↓
CLEANING
   ↓
TOKENIZATION
   ↓
EMBEDDING
   ↓
FEATURE EXTRACTION
   ↓
DATABASE
   ↓
LLM
```

The paper describes real-time ingestion, cleaning, tokenization, embeddings, feature extraction and data augmentation as parts of the pipeline. fileciteturn3file0L88-L117

---

# 8. Example: News article

Suppose you receive:

```text
"TCS announces a major new AI partnership
with a global technology company..."
```

### Step 1 — Raw data

```json
{
  "title": "...",
  "source": "Example News",
  "time": "...",
  "url": "..."
}
```

---

### Step 2 — Cleaning

Remove:

```text
HTML
Advertisements
Duplicate text
Unnecessary whitespace
Tracking parameters
```

Now:

```text
TCS announces a major new AI partnership...
```

---

### Step 3 — Identify company

We need to know:

```text
Company = TCS
Ticker = TCS.NS
```

This is related to **NER — Named Entity Recognition**.

The paper lists NER as one of the fundamental financial NLP tasks. fileciteturn3file0L205-L213

---

# 9. Sentiment Analysis

Now we ask:

```text
Is this news positive or negative?
```

FinGPT can perform financial sentiment analysis as one of its core tasks. fileciteturn3file0L214-L215

For example:

```text
News:
"TCS wins a ₹5,000 crore contract."

        ↓

FinBERT / FinGPT

        ↓

Positive
```

We can represent it numerically:

```text
Positive = 0.91
Neutral  = 0.07
Negative = 0.02
```

---

# 10. But here's where FinGPT gets VERY interesting 🔥

The paper doesn't just say:

> Ask humans to label millions of articles.

That's extremely expensive.

Instead, it proposes using **stock-price movement itself as a source of labels**.

This is a very important idea.

---

# 11. Market-driven labels

Suppose:

```text
10:00 AM

News:
"Company X wins huge contract."
```

Then we observe what happens to the stock.

```text
News
 ↓
Stock price
 ↓
+5%
```

We can say:

```text
Positive
```

If:

```text
Stock price
 ↓
-4%
```

we can say:

```text
Negative
```

If:

```text
+0.1%
```

we can classify it as:

```text
Neutral
```

The paper describes this idea using the relative stock-price change following a news item and thresholds for positive/negative/neutral labels. fileciteturn3file0L148-L157

---

# 12. This is HUGE for your project

Remember when you asked:

> "Where will I get sentiment-analysis data?"

This gives us a possible answer.

We can construct our own dataset:

```text
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ News                        │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ TCS wins major contract     │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ Timestamp                   │
│ 10:00 AM                    │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ Stock                       │
│ TCS                         │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ Price before                │
│ ₹3500                       │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ Price after                 │
│ ₹3600                       │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ Movement                    │
│ +2.85%                      │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ Label                       │
│ POSITIVE                    │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

Now we have training data.

And we don't need a human to manually label every article.

🔥 **This is one of the research ideas I would seriously consider implementing in your project.**

---

# 13. What is LoRA?

Now we reach another major concept.

Suppose we download:

```text
Llama
```

Imagine:

```text
8 billion parameters
```

You don't want to retrain all 8 billion parameters.

That's expensive.

Instead:

```text
             Llama
               │
        ┌──────┴──────┐
        │             │
   Original       LoRA adapter
   Model           ↓
   frozen       small trainable
                 parameters
```

The original model remains mostly frozen.

We train a **small adapter**.

That's called:

> **LoRA — Low-Rank Adaptation**

The paper uses LoRA as a lightweight way to adapt pretrained LLMs to finance. fileciteturn3file0L148-L167

---

# 14. Why LoRA matters to YOU

You said:

> "I want everything free."

This is exactly the direction you want.

Instead of:

```text
Train gigantic model
       ↓
$$$$$
```

we do:

```text
Open-source LLM
       +
Financial dataset
       +
LoRA
       ↓
Financially adapted model
```

Much cheaper.

The paper contrasts lightweight adaptation with the enormous cost of training a financial model from scratch. fileciteturn3file0L131-L147

---

# 15. RLSP — Reinforcement Learning on Stock Prices

This is probably the most advanced idea in the paper.

Normal RL:

```text
Agent
  ↓
Action
  ↓
Environment
  ↓
Reward
```

For example:

```text
Game
 ↓
Agent plays
 ↓
Gets reward
```

FinGPT proposes:

```text
Financial LLM
      ↓
Sentiment
      ↓
Market reaction
      ↓
Reward
      ↓
Update model
```

The **stock market becomes the environment**, and subsequent stock-price movement becomes feedback. fileciteturn3file0L168-L188

---

# 16. RAG

Now imagine your user asks:

> "Why did TCS fall today?"

Your LLM's pretrained knowledge isn't enough.

We retrieve recent information:

```text
Today's news
Today's filings
Recent earnings
Recent sentiment
Current market data
```

Then:

```text
User Question
      ↓
Retriever
      ↓
Relevant Documents
      ↓
LLM
      ↓
Answer
```

That's:

> **Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)**

The paper describes RAG as combining document retrieval with an LLM so the model generates answers using relevant external context rather than relying only on its internal knowledge. fileciteturn3file0L189-L197

---

# 17. Your project's AI assistant

Now we can directly translate FinGPT into your application:

```text
                    USER
                      │
                      ▼
              "Should I buy TCS?"
                      │
                      ▼
                  RAG SYSTEM
                      │
        ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
        ↓             ↓             ↓
      News         Market        Portfolio
        │             │             │
        ↓             ↓             ↓
   Sentiment      Indicators       Risk
        │             │             │
        └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                      ↓
                     LLM
                      ↓
              Explanation
```

That is much more useful than simply asking an LLM:

```text
"Should I buy TCS?"
```

---

# 18. What tasks can FinGPT perform?

The paper isn't only about sentiment.

It discusses:

```text
Sentiment Analysis
Summarization
NER
Information Extraction
Numerical Reasoning
Data Analysis
Terminology Understanding
Intent Detection
```

fileciteturn3file0L198-L236

This is PERFECT for your application.

For example:

### User uploads annual report

```text
PDF
 ↓
LLM
 ↓
Summary
```

### User asks

```text
"What is TCS revenue?"
```

↓

Numerical reasoning.

### User asks

```text
"What companies are mentioned?"
```

↓

NER.

### User asks

```text
"What is the market sentiment?"
```

↓

Sentiment analysis.

---

# 19. FinGPT ≠ Stock Price Prediction Model

This distinction is **very important**.

Don't make this mistake:

```text
FinGPT
   ↓
Tomorrow's price = ₹4,250
```

That's not what the paper fundamentally provides.

FinGPT is primarily a **financial language-model framework**.

Your complete application should combine:

```text
             STOCK SYSTEM
                  │
       ┌──────────┼──────────┐
       ↓          ↓          ↓
    Market      Finance      AI
     Model       NLP         LLM
       │          │           │
       ↓          ↓           ↓
   XGBoost      FinBERT     FinGPT
   LSTM         Sentiment    RAG
   TFT
```

This is the architecture I would recommend for your project.

---

# 20. So what are WE actually going to build?

Based on this paper, I would modify your earlier architecture to:

```text
                    ┌───────────────┐
                    │    USER       │
                    └───────┬───────┘
                            ↓
                     NEXT.JS WEB APP
                            ↓
                    NODE.JS BACKEND
                            ↓
       ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
       ↓                    ↓                    ↓
 MARKET DATA             NEWS DATA          USER DATA
       ↓                    ↓                    ↓
   PostgreSQL          NLP PIPELINE       PostgreSQL
       │                    │
       │              ┌─────┴──────┐
       │              ↓            ↓
       │           FinBERT       FinGPT
       │              │            │
       │              └─────┬──────┘
       │                    ↓
       │               SENTIMENT
       │                    │
       └──────────┬─────────┘
                  ↓
          FEATURE ENGINEERING
                  ↓
          ┌───────┴────────┐
          ↓                ↓
       XGBoost            LSTM
          │                │
          └───────┬────────┘
                  ↓
             PREDICTION
                  ↓
               RAG + LLM
                  ↓
          AI EXPLANATION
                  ↓
          PAPER TRADING
```

---

# 🎯 What I want you to learn from this paper

Don't try to implement everything from the paper immediately.

Understand these **7 concepts** first:

| # | Concept | Why we need it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Financial data pipeline | Collect market/news data |
| 2 | Sentiment analysis | Understand financial news |
| 3 | Market-driven labels | Create our own training data |
| 4 | LoRA | Cheap LLM fine-tuning |
| 5 | Embeddings | Search financial information |
| 6 | RAG | Give LLM current financial context |
| 7 | RLSP | Advanced market-feedback training |

The paper itself also emphasizes real-time APIs, streaming data, embeddings, RAG and prompt construction as parts of the overall framework. fileciteturn3file0L27-L35

---

# 🧑‍💻 How we'll learn it

I suggest **not** reading this paper like a college paper where you memorize every paragraph.

We'll turn it into a practical course:

### Lesson 1 — Financial AI architecture
**We're here.** ✅

### Lesson 2 — Financial data
We'll build:

```text
News API
     +
Stock API
     +
Company filings
     ↓
PostgreSQL
```

### Lesson 3 — Financial NLP

Learn:

```text
Tokenization
Embeddings
NER
Sentiment
```

### Lesson 4 — FinBERT

Actually run:

```python
text
 ↓
FinBERT
 ↓
Positive / Negative / Neutral
```

### Lesson 5 — Market-driven labels

Build our own:

```text
News → Price movement → Label
```

dataset.

### Lesson 6 — LoRA

Understand:

```text
LLM
 ↓
LoRA
 ↓
Financial LLM
```

and eventually fine-tune one.

### Lesson 7 — RAG

Build:

```text
News
Reports
Filings
   ↓
Embeddings
   ↓
Vector DB
   ↓
Retriever
   ↓
LLM
```

### Lesson 8 — RLSP

Only after we understand basic ML/RL.

### Lesson 9 — Put everything into your stock application

```text
Real-time market data
        +
Financial news
        +
FinBERT
        +
XGBoost/LSTM
        +
RAG
        +
LLM
        +
Paper trading
```

---

## 🔥 The key takeaway

If you remember **one diagram from today's lesson**, remember this:

```text
                  FINANCIAL AI
                       │
                       ▼
                 DATA SOURCES
                       │
          ┌────────────┼────────────┐
          ↓            ↓            ↓
        STOCK         NEWS        FILINGS
          │            │            │
          └────────────┼────────────┘
                       ↓
                DATA ENGINEERING
                       ↓
             ┌─────────┴─────────┐
             ↓                   ↓
        ML MODELS            FINANCIAL LLM
             │                   │
       Prediction          Understanding
             │                   │
             └─────────┬─────────┘
                       ↓
                      RAG
                       ↓
                  AI ASSISTANT
                       ↓
                PAPER TRADING
```

**That is the bridge between this research paper and the application you want to build.** 🚀

And importantly, we **don't need to implement FinGPT itself from scratch**. We can take the ideas from this paper and build a smaller, free/open-source version specifically for your project. The paper's own approach emphasizes open-source models, lightweight adaptation, real-time data pipelines, and reusable financial NLP tasks. fileciteturn2file0L31-L40

Yes. For **our exact project**, we should not collect 15 random APIs. We can keep the first version surprisingly small.

Also, when you say **“their token”**: I can tell you **which API key/token you need and where to get it**, but you should never paste your real secret keys into chat or GitHub. Put them in `.env`.

I checked the current 2026 availability/pricing because these free tiers change frequently.

# 🔑 APIs we actually need

| Purpose | API / Tool | Key needed? | Free? | Priority |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 🇮🇳 Indian live market data | **Upstox API** | Yes | Yes | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |
| 🇮🇳 Alternative Indian market data | **Angel One SmartAPI** | Yes | Yes | ⭐⭐⭐⭐ |
| 📊 Historical/backup data | **Yahoo Finance / yfinance** | No | Yes | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |
| 📰 Financial news | **NewsAPI** | Yes | Dev only | ⭐⭐⭐⭐ |
| 📰 Alternative news | **GNews** | Yes | Dev only | ⭐⭐⭐ |
| 🤖 Sentiment | **FinBERT/Hugging Face** | Optional | Yes | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |
| 🧠 LLM | **Ollama** | No | Yes/local | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |
| 🧠 Cloud LLM alternative | **OpenRouter** | Yes | Free models | ⭐⭐⭐ |
| 📈 Economic data | **FRED** | Yes | Yes | ⭐⭐⭐ |
| 🇺🇸 Company filings | **SEC EDGAR** | No API key | Yes | ⭐⭐⭐ |
| 📊 Charts | **TradingView Lightweight Charts** | No | Yes | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |
| 🧮 Technical indicators | **pandas-ta** | No | Yes | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |
| 💾 Database | PostgreSQL | No API key | Yes | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |
| ⚡ Cache/queue | Redis + BullMQ | No API key | Yes | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |

---

# 1. 🇮🇳 Upstox API — MOST IMPORTANT

For **your Indian stock application**, I'd investigate Upstox first.

Their current developer page says their trading and market-data APIs have free access and provides real-time market data through WebSockets. citeturn2search6

This gives us things like:

```text
NSE
BSE
Stocks
Quotes
OHLC
Market data
WebSocket streaming
Orders
Portfolio
```

### What credential do we need?

You'll obtain credentials from your Upstox developer application.

Typically you'll have something like:

```env
UPSTOX_CLIENT_ID=
UPSTOX_CLIENT_SECRET=
UPSTOX_ACCESS_TOKEN=
```

**Do not put your real values here.**

We'll generate the access token through their authentication flow rather than inventing one.

---

# 2. 🇮🇳 Angel One SmartAPI — Backup

This is another very interesting option.

Their current official site explicitly advertises **free APIs**, including real-time market data and trading functionality, with SDKs for Node.js, Python, Java, etc. citeturn2search4

Credentials will be generated from your SmartAPI developer account.

Something along the lines of:

```env
ANGEL_API_KEY=
ANGEL_CLIENT_CODE=
ANGEL_PASSWORD=
ANGEL_TOTP=
```

We don't need this **if Upstox works well enough**.

I'd keep it as a backup provider.

---

# 3. 📊 Yahoo Finance / yfinance

This one is beautiful for our project because:

**No API token required.**

Python:

```bash
pip install yfinance
```

Then:

```python
import yfinance as yf

data = yf.download("RELIANCE.NS", period="1y")
```

You get historical market data such as:

```text
Open
High
Low
Close
Volume
```

So:

```text
Upstox
   ↓
Live market

yfinance
   ↓
Historical/training data
```

That's a very good combination for our development stage.

**Important:** don't treat Yahoo Finance as an exchange-grade real-time feed or assume its data can be redistributed commercially.

---

# 4. 📰 NewsAPI

For development, we can use NewsAPI.

The current free Developer plan is:

```text
$0
100 requests/day
24-hour article delay
Search up to one month old
```

and is intended for development/testing, not production. citeturn0search4

You'll need:

```env
NEWS_API_KEY=
```

---

# 5. 📰 GNews

Another news source.

Current free plan:

```text
€0
100 requests/day
10 articles/request
12-hour delay
30 days historical data
```

It is also explicitly limited to development/non-commercial use on the free plan. citeturn0search2

Credential:

```env
GNEWS_API_KEY=
```

### Do we need BOTH?

No.

Start with:

```text
NewsAPI
```

Then add GNews if we need redundancy.

---

# 6. 🤖 FinBERT — Sentiment

This is **extremely important** for our research project.

And here's the good part:

### We don't necessarily need an API.

We can run FinBERT locally using:

```text
Python
+
Hugging Face Transformers
+
PyTorch
```

Architecture:

```text
News
 ↓
FinBERT
 ↓
Positive
Neutral
Negative
```

So:

```env
HF_TOKEN=
```

is **optional** if we're downloading/running the model locally.

Hugging Face does provide inference through its providers using a Hugging Face token, but for our "everything free" target I'd prefer local inference first. citeturn0search6turn0search7

---

# 7. 🧠 Ollama — Our AI Brain

For the AI chatbot, RAG, explanations, etc.:

**Ollama**

No API key.

We run:

```text
Ollama
   ↓
Qwen / Llama / Gemma
   ↓
Our application
```

For example:

```bash
ollama run qwen3
```

Then our Node/Python backend talks to Ollama locally.

So:

```env
OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434
```

No secret.

This is actually my **#1 choice for your free development environment**.

---

# 8. 🧠 OpenRouter — Optional Cloud AI

If your laptop struggles with local models, use OpenRouter as a fallback.

Current OpenRouter documentation provides free-model routing, and its current free plan lists free models with a **50 requests/day** rate limit. citeturn0search0turn0search3

Credential:

```env
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=
```

The important thing is:

```text
Ollama
  ↓
Primary

OpenRouter
  ↓
Fallback
```

That keeps your application mostly free.

---

# 9. 📈 FRED API

This isn't for stock prices.

It's for **macroeconomic data**.

For example:

```text
Interest rates
Inflation
GDP
Unemployment
Treasury yields
Economic indicators
```

FRED requires an API key for its API requests. citeturn1search0turn1search7

Credential:

```env
FRED_API_KEY=
```

Then:

```text
Stock price
+
Company fundamentals
+
News sentiment
+
Macro indicators
```

can become our ML features.

---

# 10. 🇺🇸 SEC EDGAR

This is a cool one.

For US companies:

```text
10-K
10-Q
8-K
XBRL financial data
```

And **no API key is required** for the SEC's EDGAR APIs. citeturn1search10

So:

```text
SEC
 ↓
Company financial statements
 ↓
RAG
 ↓
AI assistant
```

For an Indian-stock-focused application, this isn't essential initially. Later we can add Indian company filings/exchange disclosures through appropriate official/public sources.

---

# 11. 📊 TradingView Lightweight Charts

This is **NOT an API**.

That's important.

We don't need a token.

Install:

```bash
npm install lightweight-charts
```

Then we can display:

```text
Candlestick
─────────────

     ┌─┐
     │ │
 ┌───┘ │
 │     └──┐
 │        │
 └────────┘
```

plus:

```text
Volume
████
██████
███
████████
```

and:

```text
RSI
MACD
EMA
SMA
```

We calculate those ourselves.

---

# 12. 🧮 Technical Indicators

Again:

**No API required.**

Python:

```bash
pip install pandas-ta
```

Then:

```text
OHLCV
 ↓
pandas-ta
 ↓
RSI
MACD
EMA
SMA
ATR
ADX
Bollinger Bands
VWAP
```

This is much better than wasting API requests for something we can calculate locally.

---

# 13. What about Alpha Vantage?

Keep it as a **backup**, not our main provider.

It requires:

```env
ALPHA_VANTAGE_API_KEY=
```

They currently offer a free key, but their free service is limited to **25 requests/day**, and real-time/15-minute delayed US stock data is premium. citeturn1search2turn1search8

So I wouldn't build our architecture around it.

---

# 14. What about Twelve Data?

It's useful, but its free tier isn't ideal for our exact goal.

The current Basic plan is:

```text
$0
800 API credits/day
8 API credits/minute
8 trial WebSocket credits
```

and the free plan has restrictions around market coverage and usage. citeturn1search1turn1search6

Also, Twelve Data distinguishes between internal/non-display use and external display/commercial use, so we need to pay attention to licensing if we ever turn this into a public product. citeturn1search4

---

# 🔥 Therefore, our actual API stack

I would start with only this:

```text
┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
│             OUR STOCK APP                 │
└─────────────────────┬─────────────────────┘
                      │
        ┌─────────────┼──────────────┐
        │             │              │
        ▼             ▼              ▼
    UPSTOX         NEWS API       YFINANCE
   Live Data        News         Historical
        │             │              │
        └─────────────┼──────────────┘
                      ▼
                PostgreSQL
                      │
             ┌────────┴────────┐
             ▼                 ▼
          FinBERT          Technical TA
             │                 │
             └────────┬────────┘
                      ▼
                ML Prediction
                      │
             ┌────────┴────────┐
             ▼                 ▼
          XGBoost           LSTM
             │                 │
             └────────┬────────┘
                      ▼
                    RAG
                      │
                      ▼
                   Ollama
                      │
                      ▼
              AI STOCK ASSISTANT
```

---

# 🔐 Your `.env`

Eventually, our backend might have:

```env
# =========================
# DATABASE
# =========================
DATABASE_URL=

# =========================
# INDIAN MARKET DATA
# =========================
UPSTOX_CLIENT_ID=
UPSTOX_CLIENT_SECRET=
UPSTOX_ACCESS_TOKEN=

# =========================
# NEWS
# =========================
NEWS_API_KEY=

# Optional
GNEWS_API_KEY=

# =========================
# AI
# =========================

# Optional — only if using Hugging Face hosted inference
HF_TOKEN=

# Optional cloud LLM fallback
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=

# =========================
# ECONOMIC DATA
# =========================
FRED_API_KEY=

# =========================
# REDIS
# =========================
REDIS_URL=

# =========================
# OLLAMA
# =========================
OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434
```

**Never commit this file.**

```gitignore
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
```

And `.env.example` should contain only empty placeholders.

---

# 🏆 What I recommend YOU obtain first

Don't create 10 accounts today. 😄

Do these **in this exact order**:

### Step 1

**Upstox developer account**

→ Indian live market data

urlUpstox Trading APIhttps://upstox.com/trading-api/

### Step 2

**NewsAPI account**

→ financial news

urlNewsAPIhttps://newsapi.org/

### Step 3

**FRED account**

→ economic indicators

urlFRED API key registration/documentationhttps://fred.stlouisfed.org/docs/api/api_key.html

### Step 4

**Hugging Face account**

→ model downloads / optional hosted inference

urlHugging Facehttps://huggingface.co/

### Step 5

**Install Ollama**

→ local LLM, no API key

urlOllamahttps://ollama.com/

### Step 6

Install:

```bash
pip install yfinance pandas-ta transformers torch
```

No tokens required for those.

---

## ⚠️ One very important correction to our earlier plan

For **paper trading**, we don't actually need a broker API.

We'll create our own simulator:

```text
Virtual Cash
₹10,00,000
      ↓
BUY
      ↓
100 RELIANCE
      ↓
Current Market Price
      ↓
P&L
```

So we don't expose real-money trading at all.

Later, if you want **real broker integration**, we can add Upstox/Angel/Dhan separately.

For example, Dhan currently advertises free trading APIs, live market feeds, historical data, portfolio APIs and a sandbox, although its pricing distinguishes trading APIs from its data API offering. citeturn2search2turn2search5

---

# 🎯 Final minimum set

If our goal is **$0 development cost**, I'd start with only:

**Required**

```text
1. Upstox       → Indian market data
2. NewsAPI      → news
3. yfinance     → historical data
4. FinBERT      → sentiment
5. Ollama       → LLM
6. PostgreSQL   → database
7. Redis        → cache/queue
8. Lightweight Charts → charts
9. pandas-ta    → indicators
10. XGBoost     → prediction
```

**Optional later**

```text
11. GNews
12. FRED
13. Hugging Face hosted inference
14. OpenRouter
15. Angel One
16. Dhan
17. SEC EDGAR
```

And **you do not need API keys for every item**. Only the services marked as API providers require credentials.

### One thing I would do next

Before writing any frontend, let's build **Phase 1: Market Data Service**.

We'll take:

```text
Upstox
   ↓
API/WebSocket
   ↓
Node.js
   ↓
PostgreSQL
   ↓
React/Next.js
   ↓
TradingView-style Candlestick Chart
   ↓
Live price movement
```

Once we make **one real stock move live on your chart**, the rest of the project becomes much easier to understand. 🚀

Yep — this error is **not a Git installation problem**. GitHub is telling you that it cannot find/access this repository:

```text

```

Both commands failing confirms it:

```text
remote: Repository not found.
```

and

```text

```

### Most likely causes

#### 1. Repository name is slightly different

You have:

```text
Ai-Stock-AnlyasisSystem
```

Notice **Anlyasis** — if the actual repository is named something like:

```text
Ai-Stock-AnalysisSystem
AI-Stock-Analysis-System
Ai-Stock-AnalysisSystem
```

the URL won't work.

Go to your GitHub profile and check the exact repository name.

---

#### 2. Repository doesn't exist

Try:

```bash
gh repo list abhijeetgorhe26
```

This will show the repositories that GitHub CLI can see for that account.

You can also run:

```bash
gh repo view abhijeetgorhe26/Ai-Stock-AnlyasisSystem
```

If it says repository not found, the repo either doesn't exist under that account or you don't have access.

---

#### 3. It's a private repository and you're logged into the wrong GitHub account

Check:

```bash
gh auth status
```

You should see which GitHub account `gh` is authenticated as.

If it's not:

```text
abhijeetgorhe26
```

log out and authenticate again:

```bash
gh auth logout
gh auth login
```

Then choose:

```text
GitHub.com
HTTPS
Login with a web browser
```

---

You posted your email address in the terminal output. That's not a GitHub secret, so it's not a security emergency, but **don't share your GitHub password, PAT/token, client secret, or API keys** here.

For your AI stock project, we're going to have plenty of API credentials later, so keep them strictly in `.env`.

Run these **three commands**:

```bash

```

```bash

```

```bash
git ls-remote https://github.com/abhijeetgorhe26/Ai-Stock-AnlyasisSystem.git
```

Choose:

```text
HTTPS
```

Your Git commit identity can be different from your GitHub login, so **don't worry if these don't match exactly**. The important one for this problem is:

You did the right thing by masking most of it:

fatal: not in a git directory

Exactly — this error is simple. 😄

```text
fatal: not in a git directory
```

means you're currently in:

```text
AI System/
```

but **not inside a Git repository** yet.

### Do this

First clone the repository:

```bash
gh repo clone abhijeetgorhe26/Ai-Stock-AnlyasisSystem
```

Then enter it:

```bash
cd Ai-Stock-AnlyasisSystem
```

Now check:

```bash
git status
```

You should see something like:

```text
On branch main
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.
```

Now set your Git identity **for this project**:

```bash
git config user.name "Abhijeet Gorhe"
git config user.email "abhijeetgorhe8@gmail.com"
```

Verify:

```bash
git config user.name
git config user.email
```

Expected:

```text
Abhijeet Gorhe
abhijeetgorhe8@gmail.com
```

### Important distinction

There are two different things here:

```text
GitHub authentication
        ↓
gh auth status
        ↓
Which GitHub account you're logged into
```

versus:

```text
Git commit identity
        ↓
git config user.name
git config user.email
        ↓
Who the commit is attributed to
```

Your current error is only because `git config` without `--global` tries to modify the **current repository's local configuration**, and you're not inside a repository yet.

If you want to configure it **globally** instead, you can run this from anywhere:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Abhijeet Gorhe"
git config --global user.email "abhijeetgorhe8@gmail.com"
```

For your project, I'd use the **global configuration** unless you intentionally want different identities for different repositories.

Absolutely. For **our AI Stock Analysis + Prediction + Paper Trading platform**, I’d structure the entire project into **12 major development phases**, with smaller sub-phases inside each. This is much easier to execute than trying to build 30 disconnected phases.

The goal is:

> **Free/open-source first → working product → AI → paper trading → research-grade evaluation → production.**


[L194] \chapter*{1. Introduction}
[L195] \addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{1. Introduction}

[L197] \section*{1.1 Background}

[L199] The stock market is a dynamic financial environment in which stock prices
[L200] are influenced by historical price movements, trading volume, financial
[L201] news, company-related information, market trends, and economic conditions.
[L202] The large volume and continuously changing nature of this information makes
[L203] manual analysis difficult and time-consuming.

[L205] Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Natural Language
[L206] Processing (NLP) provide techniques for analysing large numerical and textual
[L207] datasets. Machine learning models can identify patterns in historical market
[L208] data, while NLP techniques can analyse financial news and determine its
[L209] sentiment.

[L211] The proposed project develops an integrated web-based platform for
[L212] AI-assisted stock-market analysis. It combines market data, technical
[L213] indicators, stock-price prediction, financial-news sentiment analysis,
[L214] portfolio management, interactive visualisation, and an AI chatbot in a
[L215] single application.

[L217] The system is intended to serve as an academic decision-support platform.
[L218] It will provide analytical insights to users but will not guarantee
[L219] investment returns or automatically execute real-money trades.

[L221] \section*{1.2 Motivation}

[L223] Investors generally need multiple sources to analyse a stock, including
[L224] price charts, historical data, technical indicators, financial news, and
[L225] portfolio information. Analysing these sources independently can be
[L226] difficult and time-consuming.

[L228] The motivation of this project is to integrate these different analytical
[L229] components into one platform. The system will process market information,
[L230] generate predictions, analyse financial-news sentiment, and present the
[L231] results through an interactive dashboard.

[L233] The project also aims to demonstrate the practical application of machine
[L234] learning, deep learning, natural language processing, data visualisation,
[L235] database technologies, and conversational AI in the financial domain.

[L237] \section*{1.3 Problem Statement}

[L239] Stock-market analysis requires examination of multiple numerical and textual
[L240] information sources. Analysing these sources separately can be difficult and
[L241] time-consuming.

[L243] Therefore, there is a need for an integrated AI-based application that
[L244] processes market data, technical indicators, financial news, and portfolio
[L245] information and presents the resulting analytical insights through a single
[L246] user-friendly platform.

[L278] \chapter*{3. Literature Review}
[L279] \addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{3. Literature Review}

[L281] \begin{enumerate}[
[L282] leftmargin=1.5cm,
[L283] itemsep=8pt,
[L284] topsep=4pt
]

\item
[L288] \textbf{Tetlock (2007)} -- Investigated the relationship between media
[L289] content and stock-market activity. The study demonstrated that media
[L290] information can provide useful information about investor sentiment and
[L291] market behaviour.

\item
[L294] \textbf{Bollen, Mao and Zeng (2011)} -- Studied public mood using
[L295] social-media information and its relationship with stock-market movements.
[L296] The study demonstrated the potential of sentiment information as an
[L297] additional market signal.

\item
[L300] \textbf{Nelson, Pereira and de Oliveira (2017)} -- Investigated stock-market
[L301] price movement prediction using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural
[L302] networks. The work demonstrated the application of recurrent neural networks
[L303] to sequential financial data.

\item
[L306] \textbf{Fischer and Krauss (2018)} -- Studied the application of Long
[L307] Short-Term Memory networks for financial-market prediction and demonstrated
[L308] the usefulness of deep-learning methods for sequential market information.

\item
[L311] \textbf{Rouf et al. (2021)} -- Presented a survey of machine-learning
[L312] techniques used for stock-market prediction and discussed different
[L313] methodologies, data-processing techniques, and future research directions.

\item
[L316] \textbf{Gite et al. (2021)} -- Investigated stock-price prediction using
[L317] financial-news sentiment analysis and machine-learning approaches, showing
[L318] the potential benefit of combining textual and numerical information.

\item
[L321] \textbf{Fazlija and Harder (2022)} -- Investigated the use of financial-news
[L322] sentiment for predicting stock-price direction and discussed sentiment as an
[L323] additional feature for financial prediction.

\item
[L326] \textbf{Mintarya et al. (2023)} -- Presented a systematic literature review
[L327] of machine-learning approaches used for stock-market prediction and
[L328] discussed the development of predictive models for financial data.

[L330] \end{enumerate}

[L332] \section*{3.1 Research Gap}

[L334] Existing research demonstrates the usefulness of historical market data,
[L335] machine-learning models, deep-learning models, and financial-news sentiment
[L336] for stock-market analysis.

[L338] However, there is scope for an integrated user-oriented application that
[L339] combines market-data processing, technical indicators, prediction, news
[L340] sentiment, portfolio tracking, interactive visualisation, and conversational
[L341] AI in a single platform.

[L343] The proposed project addresses this gap by integrating these components into
[L344] one web-based system and presenting analytical information through an
[L345] interactive dashboard.

[L497] The project scope includes user registration and authentication, stock
[L498] search, historical market-data processing, interactive charts, technical

[L500] portfolio tracking, AI-assisted interaction, dashboard visualisation,

[L503] The system will provide analytical information for selected stocks and
[L504] markets. The scope includes experimentation and comparison of different
[L505] machine-learning and deep-learning approaches.

[L507] The project will not include direct execution of real-money trades,

[L522] \section*{7.1 System Architecture / Approach}

[L524] The proposed AI-Based Stock Market Prediction and Investment Assistant
[L525] follows a modular architecture consisting of the frontend, backend,
[L526] database, market-data services, news-processing services, AI/ML modules,
[L527] portfolio management, and AI assistant.

[L529] The system collects historical and available market information and processes
[L530] it using data-preprocessing and feature-engineering techniques. Machine
[L531] learning and deep learning models are then used for predictive analysis.
[L532] Financial news is processed using Natural Language Processing for sentiment
[L533] analysis. The resulting information is presented to the user through an
[L534] interactive dashboard.

[L645] \subsection*{7.1.2 PEAS Description}

[L647] \begin{itemize}[
[L648] leftmargin=1.5cm,
[L649] itemsep=6pt
]

\item
[L653] \textbf{Performance Measure:}
[L654] Accurate stock-price prediction, low prediction error, fast response time,
[L655] appropriate Buy/Sell/Hold model outputs, portfolio-analysis quality, and
[L656] user satisfaction.

\item
[L659] \textbf{Environment:}
[L660] Stock-market information, historical market data, financial news, market
[L661] indicators, economic information, and user portfolio information.

\item
[L664] \textbf{Actuators:}
[L665] Display stock predictions, present analytical indicators, show model-generated
[L666] Buy/Sell/Hold outputs, update dashboards, generate reports and alerts, and
[L667] respond to user queries through the AI assistant.

\item
[L670] \textbf{Sensors:}
[L671] Stock-market data sources, financial-news sources, historical databases,
[L672] technical indicators, user inputs, portfolio information, and sentiment
data.

[L675] \end{itemize}

[L677] \subsection*{7.1.3 Data Processing Pipeline}

[L679] The proposed data-processing pipeline consists of the following stages:

[L681] \begin{enumerate}[
[L682] leftmargin=1.5cm,
[L683] itemsep=6pt
]

\item
[L687] Data collection from available market and financial-news sources.

\item
[L690] Data cleaning and handling of missing or inconsistent records.

\item
[L693] Data transformation and normalization.

\item
[L696] Feature engineering using price, volume, and technical indicators.

\item
[L699] Text preprocessing for financial-news analysis.

\item
[L702] Machine-learning and deep-learning model processing.

\item
[L705] Financial-news sentiment analysis.

\item
[L708] Integration of prediction, sentiment, and portfolio information.

\item
[L711] Dashboard visualisation and report generation.

[L713] \end{enumerate}

[L715] \subsection*{7.1.4 Stock Prediction Module}

[L717] The prediction module will investigate different machine-learning and
[L718] deep-learning approaches. Candidate models include Random Forest, XGBoost,
[L719] and LSTM.

[L721] Historical stock-market data will be divided into training and evaluation
[L722] datasets. The models will be trained using selected features and evaluated
[L723] using suitable performance measures such as Mean Absolute Error (MAE),
[L724] Mean Squared Error (MSE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), and directional
[L725] accuracy where applicable.

[L727] \subsection*{7.1.5 Financial News Sentiment Module}

[L729] Financial-news articles will be processed using Natural Language Processing
[L730] techniques. The system will extract relevant textual information and classify
[L731] the sentiment of financial news into categories such as positive, neutral,
[L732] or negative.

[L734] A finance-oriented language model such as FinBERT may be investigated for
[L735] financial sentiment classification. The generated sentiment score can be
[L736] presented together with stock information and may be incorporated as an
[L737] additional feature in analytical models.

[L739] \subsection*{7.1.6 Portfolio Management Module}

[L741] The portfolio module will allow users to maintain information about their
[L742] holdings and transactions.

[L744] The system will maintain information such as:

[L746] \begin{itemize}[
[L747] leftmargin=1.5cm,
[L748] itemsep=5pt
]

[L751] \item Stock name
[L752] \item Quantity
[L753] \item Transaction type
[L754] \item Transaction price
[L755] \item Transaction date
[L756] \item Current value
[L757] \item Profit/Loss

[L759] \end{itemize}

[L761] The module will provide a summarized view of the user's portfolio.

[L763] \subsection*{7.1.7 AI Assistant}

[L765] The AI assistant will provide a conversational interface through which users
[L766] can ask questions about stock-related analytical information.

[L768] The assistant may provide explanations regarding:

[L770] \begin{itemize}[
[L771] leftmargin=1.5cm,
[L772] itemsep=5pt
]

[L775] \item Stock prediction results
[L776] \item Technical indicators
[L777] \item Financial-news sentiment
[L778] \item Portfolio statistics
[L779] \item Market trends
[L780] \item System-generated analytical insights

[L782] \end{itemize}

[L784] The assistant will provide explanations based on available system
[L785] information and will not guarantee investment outcomes.

[L1438] \addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{9. Feasibility Study}

[L1440] \section*{9.1 Technical Feasibility}

[L1442] The project is technically feasible because the required programming
[L1443] languages, frameworks, machine-learning libraries, NLP tools, database
[L1444] technologies, and development environments are widely available.

[L1446] The modular architecture allows the project team to develop, test, and
[L1447] integrate individual components independently.

[L1449] \section*{9.2 Economic Feasibility}

[L1451] The prototype can primarily be developed using open-source software and
[L1452] libraries. No specialised hardware is required for the basic implementation.

[L1454] The project will use suitable freely available or permitted data sources
[L1455] where possible. Any external service will be selected according to its
[L1456] availability, usage limits, and applicable terms.

[L1458] \section*{9.3 Operational Feasibility}

[L1460] The system is designed as a centralized dashboard so that users can access
[L1461] stock information, predictions, sentiment, portfolio statistics, and AI
[L1462] assistance from one application.

[L1464] The proposed interface is intended to be simple and user-friendly so that
[L1465] users can perform stock analysis without switching between multiple
[L1466] applications.

[L1468] The system is intended as an academic decision-support application and will
[L1469] not autonomously execute real-money trades.

Yep — I checked the **actual `main.tex` content you uploaded**, not just the error messages. The main issue is that your file contains **two different LaTeX document preambles merged together**. For example, it has an `article` class and then a second `report` class, plus duplicate `geometry`, `hyperref`, etc. fileciteturn7file0L1-L12

I fixed the file and **compiled it successfully**. It produces a **10-page PDF**.

### What was actually wrong

| Error | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Two `\documentclass` | `article` + `report` both present | Keep only `report` |
| Geometry option clash | `geometry` loaded twice with different options | Keep one |
| Hyperref option clash | `hyperref` loaded twice | Keep one |
| `pgfkeys` runaway | Broken/unused TikZ configuration | Removed unused TikZ block |
| `fevicon.png not found` | Image doesn't exist | Made image optional |
| `There's no line here to end` | `\\[30pt]` after `tabular` | Changed to `\vspace{30pt}` |
| `headheight too small` | Fancy header needs more height | Set `14pt` |
| `\toprule undefined` | `booktabs` wasn't loaded in the remaining preamble | Added `\usepackage{booktabs}` |
| Overfull `\hbox` | Long text/URLs | Warning only; document still compiles |

Your original duplicate preamble is visible right at the beginning of the file. fileciteturn7file0L1-L43

The missing favicon and invalid line break are also directly in the uploaded file. fileciteturn7file0L148-L190

### One important thing

The following are **not compilation errors anymore**:

```text
Overfull \hbox
Underfull \hbox
```

They are layout warnings. Your PDF successfully generated despite them.

The long URL in the References section is responsible for one of the overfull boxes. fileciteturn7file0L620-L643

### Your corrected file

I compiled the corrected version successfully:

**[Download the corrected main.tex](sandbox:/mnt/data/main_fixed.tex)**

**[Download the compiled PDF](sandbox:/mnt/data/main_fixed.pdf)**

You can replace your current `main.tex` with `main_fixed.tex`.

One small caveat: I removed the TikZ configuration because **there are no TikZ diagrams actually being used in the current document**, so keeping that configuration was unnecessary and was causing the `pgfkeys` failure. The actual project material/content was left intact.
